content.title: Prolonged infectivity of murine norovirus in aerosols suggests potential for airborne transmission.
content.abstract: BACKGROUND: Norovirus is a highly contagious enteric virus best known for fecal-oral transmission, but increasing evidence suggests that airborne spread may also contribute to outbreaks. Aerosol transmission of norovirus can occur during episodes involving vomiting, diarrhoea, or toilet flushing. AIM: To investigate this possibility, the infectivity of aerosolized murine norovirus (MNV) was evaluated over time using influenza A virus (H1N1), a well-established respiratory virus transmitted via aerosols, as a reference control. METHODS: Aerosols with a mass median aerodynamic diameter of 2.38 μm were generated in a 220 L chamber and captured using gelatin filters. FINDINGS: MNV infectivity decreased by 2.33 log10 within the first 3 h but remained detectable for up to 9 h, corresponding to a total reduction of 4.2 log10. In contrast, H1N1 exhibited a more rapid decay, with a 2.9 log10 reduction within 3 h. CONCLUSION: Overall, these results indicate that MNV retains airborne infectivity for longer durations, supporting the plausibility of aerosol transmission during norovirus outbreak scenarios.
